name: Strait of Gibraltar
what: The 14 km gap between Europe and Africa that joins the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.
why: Whoever holds it decides who enters the Mediterranean; Carthage, the Umayyads, Spain and Britain all fought for it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Gibraltar (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Bosporus
what: The narrow strait at Constantinople between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara.
why: It made Constantinople rich and nearly impregnable for 1,500 years, and it is still Russia's only warm-water exit.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Bosporus (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Dardanelles
what: The Hellespont, joining the Sea of Marmara to the Aegean; Troy guarded its mouth.
why: Xerxes bridged it, Athens's grain came through it, and the Allies failed to force it at Gallipoli in 1915.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Dardanelles (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Strait of Hormuz
what: The exit of the Persian Gulf, about 40 km wide at its narrowest.
why: About a fifth of the world's oil passes through it; Hormuz island was a great medieval trade port.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Hormuz (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Bab-el-Mandeb
what: The "Gate of Grief" between Arabia and the Horn of Africa, joining the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
why: The southern door of the Red Sea route from India to Egypt and, since 1869, to the Suez Canal.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Bab-el-Mandeb (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Strait of Malacca
what: The long channel between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula.
why: The main sea road between the Indian Ocean and China; Srivijaya, Malacca, Portugal, the Dutch and Britain each rose by holding it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Malacca (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Sunda Strait
what: The strait between Java and Sumatra, beside Krakatoa.
why: The Dutch East India Company's route to Batavia and the alternative to Malacca.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Sunda Strait (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Suez Canal
what: A sea-level canal across the isthmus of Suez, opened in 1869.
why: It cut the voyage from Europe to India by about 7,000 km and drew Britain into Egypt; the 1956 crisis ended Britain's great-power pretensions.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Suez Canal (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Panama Canal
what: A lock canal across the Isthmus of Panama, opened in 1914.
why: It joined the Atlantic and Pacific and made the United States a two-ocean naval power.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Panama Canal (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Strait of Dover
what: The narrowest point of the English Channel, 33 km wide.
why: Britain's moat: the Armada, Napoleon and Hitler all needed to cross it and none did.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Dover (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Oresund
what: The sound between Denmark and Sweden, the main entrance to the Baltic.
why: Denmark charged the Sound Dues on every passing ship from 1429 to 1857.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Oresund (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Strait of Messina
what: The 3 km strait between Sicily and mainland Italy, home of Scylla and Charybdis.
why: The First Punic War began over Messina, and every power in the central Mediterranean has had to hold it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Messina (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Strait of Otranto
what: The mouth of the Adriatic between Italy and Albania.
why: Venice's lifeline to the east; the Allies blockaded the Austrian fleet here in the First World War.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Strait of Otranto (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Korea Strait
what: The strait between Korea and Japan, with Tsushima in the middle.
why: The invasion road both ways: the Mongols in 1274 and 1281, Hideyoshi in 1592, and Tsushima in 1905.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Korea Strait (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Taiwan Strait
what: The 130 km strait between Taiwan and mainland China.
why: Koxinga crossed it to expel the Dutch in 1662; since 1949 it has separated two Chinas.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Taiwan Strait (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Cape of Good Hope
what: The rocky headland at the south-west tip of Africa.
why: Rounded by Dias in 1488, it opened the sea route to India; the Dutch and then the British held the Cape to guard it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cape of Good Hope (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Cape Horn and Drake Passage
what: The stormy southern tip of South America and the passage to Antarctica.
why: The only sea route between the Atlantic and Pacific until 1914, and a graveyard of ships.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cape Horn and Drake Passage (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Kerch Strait
what: The Cimmerian Bosporus, joining the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov.
why: Greek grain cities grew on its shores; it still decides access to the Sea of Azov.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Kerch Strait (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Khyber Pass
what: The mountain pass between the Afghan plateau and the plains of the Indus.
why: The gate of India: Persians, Alexander's generals, Kushans, Ghaznavids and Babur came through here or nearby.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Khyber Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Bolan Pass
what: A pass through the Toba Kakar range from Kandahar toward the Indus.
why: The southern alternative to the Khyber for armies and caravans entering India.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Bolan Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Thermopylae
what: The "Hot Gates", a narrow coastal path between mountains and sea in central Greece.
why: The only easy road from northern into southern Greece, defended in 480 BCE, 279 BCE and 191 BCE.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Thermopylae (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Isthmus of Corinth
what: The 6 km neck of land joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece.
why: Corinth grew rich hauling ships across it on the diolkos; Greeks walled it against Persians and Slavs.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Isthmus of Corinth (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Brenner Pass
what: The lowest main pass over the Alps between Italy and Austria.
why: The road German emperors took to Rome, and the main north-south route through the Alps.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Brenner Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Great St Bernard Pass
what: A high Alpine pass between the Aosta valley and the Rhone.
why: Napoleon crossed it in 1800 before Marengo; Roman legions and medieval pilgrims used it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Great St Bernard Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Roncevaux Pass
what: A pass over the western Pyrenees between France and Navarre.
why: Charlemagne's rearguard died here in 778, the story of the Song of Roland.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Roncevaux Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Cilician Gates
what: A pass through the Taurus Mountains from the Anatolian plateau to the Cilician plain.
why: Cyrus the Younger, Alexander and the Crusaders all marched through it toward Syria.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Cilician Gates (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Darial Gorge
what: The main pass through the central Caucasus.
why: The "Caspian Gates" of legend that Alexander was said to have closed against the northern nomads.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Darial Gorge (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Caspian Gates at Derbent
what: The narrow strip between the Caucasus and the Caspian Sea, walled by the Sasanians.
why: Persians, Arabs and Khazars fought over this wall against the steppe for centuries.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Caspian Gates at Derbent (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Dzungarian Gate
what: A windy valley between the Dzungarian Alatau and the Barlik mountains.
why: The steppe highway between Mongolia and Kazakhstan, used by Turks and Mongols heading west.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Dzungarian Gate (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Hexi Corridor
what: A strip of oases between the Tibetan plateau and the Gobi.
why: The Silk Road's Chinese end; Han, Tang and Ming all fought nomads and Tibetans for it.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Hexi Corridor (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Jade Gate (Yumen Pass)
what: The Han dynasty frontier post at the western end of the Great Wall.
why: The point where China ended and the Western Regions began.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Jade Gate (Yumen Pass) (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Shanhai Pass
what: The gate where the Great Wall meets the sea, between Manchuria and the North China Plain.
why: In 1644 its commander opened it to the Manchus, who went on to found the Qing.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Shanhai Pass (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Wakhan Corridor
what: A thin finger of Afghanistan between Tajikistan and Pakistan, reaching China.
why: Drawn in the Great Game as a buffer so Russian and British India would not touch.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Wakhan Corridor (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Fulda Gap
what: Lowland corridors through the hills of central Germany.
why: NATO expected a Soviet tank attack here throughout the Cold War.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Fulda Gap (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Iron Gates
what: The Danube's gorge through the Carpathians between Serbia and Romania.
why: Trajan built a road and bridge here to conquer Dacia; it divided Ottoman and Habsburg Europe.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Iron Gates (written from general knowledge; check)

name: First Cataract of the Nile
what: Granite rapids at Aswan that blocked river boats.
why: The ancient southern border of Egypt, beyond which lay Nubia.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: First Cataract of the Nile (written from general knowledge; check)

name: Persian Gates
what: A narrow pass in the Zagros on the road to Persepolis.
why: Ariobarzanes held Alexander here in 330 BCE until shepherds showed a way round.
